issues.legal_issue: A person’s conduct may be relevant under the relationship-opinion rule when it expresses a belief about the relationship and the person has special means of knowledge, but mere gossip, hearsay, or general reputation without conduct is insufficient.
material_facts: The disputed issue was whether the mothers of the claimants were daughters of the former owner and whether the claimants were related to him through them.
Witnesses with special means of knowledge of the family attended marriages and other family ceremonies involving the alleged daughters and grandchildren.
The witnesses’ attendance was not that of casual invitees and was treated as conduct expressing their belief about the family relationships.
issues.conclusion: The witnesses’ evidence about their attendance at the family ceremonies was admissible under section 50 as conduct expressing their opinion about the relationships; mere general reputation without conduct would not suffice.
issues.legal_principle: Section 50 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 makes relevant an opinion about a relationship when expressed by conduct of a person with special means of knowledge. “Opinion” means a judgment or belief, not merely the repetition of gossip or hearsay; the conduct must be of a kind that indicates the belief. The Court approved Chandu Lal Agarwala v. Khalilay Rahman and followed Lakshmi Reddi v. Venkata Reddi in rejecting mere general reputation without conduct. It also referred to Sitaji v. Bijendra Narain Choudhary on a family member’s independent opinion, even if based on information from deceased persons, when expressed by conduct.

predicates.relationship_in_issue: The court had to determine whether one person was related to another.
predicates.witness_has_special_means_of_knowledge: A witness had special means of knowing about the relationship at issue.
predicates.conduct_expresses_relationship_belief: The witness’s conduct was of a kind that indicated a belief about the relationship, rather than merely repeating gossip or hearsay.

issues.definition: When a relationship is in issue, conduct indicating the belief of a person with special means of knowledge makes that person’s relationship opinion relevant.

issues.legal_issue: Oral evidence of conduct expressing a relationship opinion may be given by the person whose conduct expressed the opinion or by another person who personally perceived that conduct.
material_facts: The witnesses testified to attending marriages and other ceremonies in the family whose relationships were disputed.
Their testimony concerned outward events they had personally seen or participated in, rather than direct observation of the births or other events establishing the relationships themselves.
The appellant argued that the evidence was hearsay and that only the person whose opinion was expressed by conduct could prove it.
issues.conclusion: The witnesses’ evidence about the conduct was direct evidence within section 60 and was admissible; section 50 does not require that only the person whose conduct expressed the opinion may prove it.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 50 and 60 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 operate together: the relevant item under section 50 is the external conduct expressing an opinion, and oral testimony about that conduct is direct when given by a person who personally perceived it. Either the person whose conduct is relied on or another person acquainted with and personally perceiving the conduct may prove it. The Court disapproved the contrary limitation suggested in Queen Empress v. Subbarayan.

predicates.relationship_opinion_conduct_is_relied_o: A party relied on outward conduct as expressing a person’s opinion about a relationship.
predicates.conduct_is_perceptible: The conduct consisted of external events capable of being perceived.
predicates.witness_personally_perceived_conduct: The witness personally saw, heard, or otherwise perceived the conduct about which the witness testified.

issues.definition: When outward conduct is relied on to express a relationship opinion, testimony from a person who personally perceived that conduct is direct evidence.

issues.legal_issue: A deceased person’s statement about a blood relationship may be admitted despite being made jointly with living persons when it is attributable to the deceased and the statutory conditions concerning the relationship, special knowledge, and timing are met.
material_facts: A petition in an earlier suit contained a pedigree asserting that the former owner had three daughters and identifying the descendants of two of them.
The petition was signed by one person on his own behalf and on behalf of his brothers; the signatory had died, while the brothers were alive.
The earlier suit concerned whether an alienation by the estate holder bound the reversioners, not whether the alleged daughters were related to the former owner.
The sons of a half-sister did not become preferential heirs until a later change in the law, so the precise relationship question in the present suit had not arisen when the petition was made.
Other evidence independently supported that the deceased signatory was a descendant of the former owner and had special means of knowledge of the relationship.
issues.conclusion: The pedigree statements in the petition were admissible under section 32(5); they were statements of the deceased signatory, or at least as much his statements as those of the living signatories, and were made before the precise relationship question in dispute had arisen.
issues.legal_principle: Section 32(5) of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 requires a statement by a person who is dead or otherwise unavailable, relating to a blood, marriage, or adoption relationship about which that person had special means of knowledge, and made before the question in dispute was raised. A statement signed by one person for himself and on behalf of others may be treated as that deceased person’s statement; even if joint, it may be as much the deceased person’s statement as the living persons’. The Court approved Chandra Nath Roy v. Nilamadhab Bhattacharjee. It considered Subbiah Mudaliar v. Gopala Mudaliar on the need for independent support for special means of knowledge, and distinguished the contention based on Naraini Kuar v. Chandi Din because the precise relationship dispute had not arisen in the earlier litigation.

rule.if: relationship_dispute_in_civil_proceeding and declarant_unavailable and statement_concerns_relationship and declarant_had_special_means_of_knowledge and statement_preceded_precise_dispute

predicates.relationship_dispute_in_civil_proceeding: A civil proceeding required the court to decide whether people were related by blood, marriage, or adoption.
predicates.declarant_unavailable: The person who made the statement had died or was otherwise unavailable to give evidence.
predicates.statement_concerns_relationship: The statement addressed the existence of a relationship between people.
predicates.declarant_had_special_means_of_knowledge: The person who made the statement had special means of knowing about the relationship.
predicates.statement_preceded_precise_dispute: The statement was made before the precise relationship question in dispute had arisen, even if some other related litigation was underway.
predicates.joint_statement_attributable_to_deceased: The statement was made by the unavailable person on their own behalf or jointly in a way that made it as much their statement as the statements of living persons.

issues.definition: A relationship statement in a civil proceeding is admissible when it is attributable to an unavailable declarant with special means of knowledge and predates the precise dispute.
